messages.content: I want to develop unsupervised speech recognition accent adaptation that separates pronunciation shifts from speaker and channel variation, without sacrificing existing accents. The targets are to reduce unseen-accent word error rate by at least 15% relative to a frozen recognizer using only unlabeled adaptation speech, while limiting existing-accent WER increases to one percentage point when speakers and channels vary independently.

That sets two requirements for the adaptation: improve recognition of the unseen accent using unlabeled adaptation speech, and preserve performance on existing accents. The unseen-accent target is a relative WER reduction against the frozen recognizer. The existing-accent limit is an increase of no more than one percentage point in WER, including when speaker and channel variation are not tied to one another.
Can you unpack what it means to separate pronunciation shifts from the other variation?

A pronunciation shift is the accent-related part of how words are spoken. Speaker variation reflects differences among people, while channel variation reflects differences in how speech is captured or conveyed. The aim is for adaptation to respond to the pronunciation shift rather than treating every difference in speaker or channel as evidence of a new pronunciation pattern. That describes the intended distinction, not a claim that it has already been achieved or that a particular separation method has been chosen.
Why does that distinction matter to the goal?

The desired change is better recognition of an unseen accent. If adaptation responds indiscriminately to speaker or channel differences, it may not isolate the pronunciation changes it is meant to handle. The goal therefore couples the unseen-accent improvement with protection for existing accents: a gain on the unseen accent should not come with existing-accent WER increases beyond the stated one-percentage-point limit.
When you say at least 15% relative to the frozen recognizer, is that a 15-percentage-point drop?

No. It is a relative reduction of at least 15% in unseen-accent WER. If the frozen recognizer’s unseen-accent WER is represented by W, the target is an adapted WER of at most 0.85 × W. For a purely illustrative baseline WER of 20%, that would mean 17% or lower—a three-percentage-point drop, which is 15% of the baseline. The example is not a reported measurement.
And the one-percentage-point limit is measured differently?

Yes. That limit concerns the absolute change in existing-accent WER, expressed in percentage points. As an illustration, if an existing-accent WER were 8% before adaptation, 9% would be a one-percentage-point increase; 9.2% would exceed the limit. Those numbers are examples only. The requirement itself is to limit existing-accent WER increases to one percentage point.
Does “without sacrificing existing accents” mean there can be no increase at all?

The numerical requirement allows an increase of up to one percentage point. So “without sacrificing existing accents” should be read alongside that stated tolerance, rather than as an additional zero-increase condition. An improvement or no increase would also be consistent with the limit.
What does the independently varying speakers and channels condition add?

It means the existing-accent protection has to hold in a setting where speaker and channel can change separately. The limit is not restricted to a situation in which a particular speaker always appears through a particular channel, or where either source of variation stays fixed. It also reinforces the distinction the adaptation is meant to make: a change in who is speaking and a change in recording or transmission conditions should not simply be folded into the accent-related pronunciation shift.
Are we saying speaker and channel variation must follow some particular statistical distribution?

No distribution is specified. “Independently varying” describes the condition that speakers and channels are allowed to vary separately; it does not, on its own, prescribe a statistical model, sampling scheme, or particular set of recordings.
Does the one-percentage-point rule apply to every individual speaker-channel combination?

The stated requirement limits existing-accent WER increases under independently varying speakers and channels, but it does not specify that the bound is calculated separately for every individual speaker-channel combination. It is important to retain the speaker-and-channel condition without adding an unstated rule about the level at which WER must be aggregated.
How should I interpret “using only unlabeled adaptation speech”? Does it mean the entire recognizer has never used labels?

The condition is about the speech used for adaptation: it is unlabeled, so the unseen-accent improvement cannot depend on transcripts or other labels for that adaptation speech. It does not say that the existing recognizer was originally built without labeled data, or specify how it was built. The frozen recognizer serves as the comparison baseline for the unseen-accent WER target.
Is the frozen recognizer itself what gets adapted?

The wording identifies a frozen recognizer as the baseline against which the unseen-accent WER reduction is measured. It does not specify the adaptation architecture or which components, if any, would change in an adapted system. What matters for the stated comparison is that the baseline recognizer remains fixed as a reference.
Would a particular technique for separating speaker, channel, and pronunciation effects already be implied?

No particular technique is specified. The goal describes the distinction the adaptation should make and the outcomes it should satisfy, not an implementation choice. A proposed technique would still need to be assessed against both numerical requirements: at least 15% relative unseen-accent WER reduction using only unlabeled adaptation speech, and no more than a one-percentage-point existing-accent WER increase under independently varying speakers and channels.
So an unseen-accent gain by itself would not cover the full objective?

Correct. The unseen-accent gain is necessary but not sufficient for the stated goal. The adaptation is also meant to avoid sacrificing existing accents within the specified one-percentage-point WER tolerance, even as speaker and channel vary separately. Both conditions matter; neither replaces the other.

I have a possible approach: train a pronunciation LoRA on confidence-filtered pseudo-transcripts with speaker and channel adversaries, then gate adaptation by accent prototypes, retaining frozen decoding otherwise.

That is a proposal for separating the accent-related change from other variation while limiting where adaptation is applied. The pronunciation LoRA is the proposed adaptation component. Confidence-filtered pseudo-transcripts would provide a training signal without transcripts for the adaptation speech; speaker and channel adversaries are intended to discourage the adaptation from relying on those sources of variation. The accent-prototype gate would choose when to use adaptation, with frozen decoding retained otherwise. None of those effects is established merely by proposing the components.
What role does the LoRA play here?

LoRA is the proposed trainable adaptation component, described here as a pronunciation LoRA because the change it is meant to capture is accent-related pronunciation. The proposal does not specify which recognizer components receive LoRA updates or how those updates are configured. Calling it a pronunciation LoRA states its intended role, not proof that it will respond only to pronunciation.
How can pseudo-transcripts fit an unsupervised adaptation goal?

Pseudo-transcripts are proposed text hypotheses for the adaptation speech, not supplied ground-truth transcripts. Training on them can therefore be part of an approach that uses unlabeled adaptation speech. The distinction matters: treating generated hypotheses as a training signal does not turn them into verified labels, and the proposal does not claim that they are always correct.
And why filter them by confidence?

The proposal uses confidence filtering to select which pseudo-transcripts contribute to training. Conceptually, that can avoid treating every hypothesis as equally dependable. It does not guarantee that retained hypotheses are correct, and no confidence measure or cutoff is specified here.
Could filtering alone ensure that the LoRA learns pronunciation rather than speaker identity?

No such guarantee is stated. Confidence filtering concerns the proposed pseudo-transcripts used for training. The separate concern—whether the adaptation captures pronunciation instead of speaker or channel variation—is why the proposal also includes speaker and channel adversaries. Those components have different intended roles, and their inclusion does not by itself establish that the separation succeeds.
What are the speaker and channel adversaries supposed to do?

They are intended to push the learned adaptation away from encoding distinctions attributable to the speaker or the channel, so that accent-related pronunciation shifts can be handled more distinctly. That is the purpose of including both adversaries. The proposal does not specify their training targets, loss functions, or how any speaker or channel information needed for them would be obtained.
Does including adversaries imply that the adaptation speech must have speaker and channel labels?

The proposal does not say that labeled adaptation speech is available, and the goal remains to use only unlabeled adaptation speech. It also does not spell out how the adversaries would be trained. Their intended function is clear, but their supervision and implementation cannot be filled in as settled details from this proposal alone.
Why have two adversaries instead of treating all nuisance variation as one thing?

The proposal explicitly names speaker and channel adversaries, matching the two distinct kinds of non-pronunciation variation in the goal. A speaker difference and a channel difference need not occur together; speakers and channels may vary independently. Naming both makes the intended separation explicit without asserting that either adversary will perfectly remove its respective influence.
How does the accent-prototype gate fit with the LoRA?

The LoRA is the proposed adaptation to train; the gate controls whether adaptation is used for decoding. Accent prototypes are the proposed basis for that decision. When the gate selects adaptation, the pronunciation adaptation would be used; otherwise, the proposal retains frozen decoding. It does not specify how prototypes are defined, how a match is judged, or whether the gate will always make the desired choice.
Does “otherwise” mean using a weaker version of the adaptation?

No. In this proposal, “retaining frozen decoding otherwise” means keeping the frozen decoding path when the accent-prototype gate does not select adaptation. It is a distinction between applying the proposed adaptation and retaining frozen decoding, not a stated scale of partial adaptation.
Is the gate primarily about the unseen-accent target or protecting existing accents?

It has a potential role in both parts of the goal. Selecting adaptation where appropriate is relevant to improving unseen-accent recognition, while retaining frozen decoding otherwise is intended to avoid applying an accent-specific change indiscriminately, including where existing accents are concerned. That explains the design rationale; it is not a claim that the gate achieves either WER requirement.
Could we say frozen decoding guarantees the existing-accent WER limit?

Not from this proposal alone. Frozen decoding is retained on the gate’s non-adaptation path, but the proposal does not establish how often that path would be chosen for existing accents or how the resulting WER would compare. The existing-accent requirement remains an increase of no more than one percentage point under independently varying speakers and channels.
What would distinguish an intended pronunciation response from responding to a changed microphone or speaker?

Conceptually, the intended response follows accent-related pronunciation shifts rather than speaker or channel differences. The speaker/channel adversaries are proposed to encourage that distinction during training, and the accent-prototype gate is proposed to restrict when adaptation affects decoding. Neither component supplies a demonstrated distinction on its own in the information given here.
Does the proposal change either numerical target?

No. It is an approach aimed at the same targets: at least a 15% relative reduction in unseen-accent word error rate compared with the frozen recognizer, using only unlabeled adaptation speech, while limiting existing-accent WER increases to one percentage point under independently varying speakers and channels. The proposal specifies a possible route toward those outcomes; it does not report that they have been achieved.
If the pseudo-transcripts are uncertain, should I describe the training signal as labeled speech?

It would be more precise to call it confidence-filtered pseudo-transcript training on unlabeled adaptation speech. That preserves the distinction between generated hypotheses and provided transcripts. It also avoids implying that confidence filtering has converted uncertain hypotheses into ground truth.
Can the accent prototypes be described as a list of known accent labels?

Not on the information in the proposal. It calls for gating adaptation by accent prototypes but does not say that the prototypes are labeled accent categories, how many exist, or how they are constructed. The supported description is their role as the basis of the gate, with frozen decoding retained when adaptation is not selected.

So the compact statement is: train the pronunciation LoRA using confidence-filtered pseudo-transcripts, use speaker/channel adversaries to discourage learning those variations, and apply adaptation through an accent-prototype gate while keeping frozen decoding otherwise?

Yes—that conveys the proposed roles without claiming a completed result. The pseudo-transcripts provide a proposed training signal from unlabeled adaptation speech; the two adversaries target speaker and channel variation; and the accent-prototype gate determines whether adaptation or frozen decoding is used. Whether that combination meets the unseen-accent improvement and existing-accent protection requirements remains open.
Can accent-prototype distances trigger the pronunciation LoRA without false activations when speakers and microphones change independently?

That is an open question for the proposed gate, not an established property of accent-prototype distances. The desired behavior is for the distances to support a pronunciation-related trigger, rather than a trigger caused merely by a different speaker or microphone. If those other changes affect the distances enough to select adaptation, the gate could falsely activate the pronunciation LoRA.
What counts as a false activation here?

It would mean the gate selects the pronunciation LoRA when the reason for the changed distance is not an accent-related pronunciation shift that calls for that adaptation. For example, a speaker or microphone change alone should not be mistaken for the pronunciation cue the gate is intended to recognize. This describes the concern; it does not assert that any such activation has occurred.
If the prototypes are called accent prototypes, doesn't that mean distance to them measures accent?

The name describes what the prototypes are intended to represent. It does not guarantee that distances to them are insensitive to speaker or microphone differences. For the gate to work as intended, the information used to calculate those distances would need to distinguish accent-related pronunciation from those other sources of variation.
Why emphasize that speakers and microphones change independently?

Because a gate might appear to track accent when speaker and microphone changes happen together, even if it is actually responding to one of those changes. When they can change separately, the question is whether either change by itself can shift a prototype distance enough to trigger the LoRA. The condition makes the intended distinction more demanding without specifying a particular test or result.
So a new speaker on the same microphone and the same speaker on a new microphone are both relevant?

Yes, as conceptual cases of independent variation. In each case, a change unrelated to pronunciation could affect the gate. The question is whether accent-prototype distances remain useful for selecting pronunciation adaptation without treating either kind of change alone as a reason to activate it.
Would keeping frozen decoding otherwise resolve the false-activation concern?

It provides a path that does not use the LoRA when the gate declines adaptation. It does not resolve the concern when the gate activates incorrectly: in that case, the system would use the pronunciation LoRA rather than retain frozen decoding. The reliability of the distance-based decision is therefore central to the question.
Could an apparent accent match still be a microphone effect?

Potentially. A distance that looks favorable to an accent prototype is not, by itself, proof of why it took that value. If microphone variation influences the information used by the gate, it could contribute to an apparent match. The same caution applies to speaker variation.
Is this asking whether the speaker and channel adversaries solve the gating problem?

It is related, but narrower. The question asks whether accent-prototype distances can trigger the pronunciation LoRA without false activations under independent speaker and microphone changes. The proposed adversaries are meant to discourage speaker and channel variation in the adaptation, but their presence does not establish that the prototype distances or the gate are immune to those variations.
Can I phrase the desired property as invariance to every difference between people and microphones?

That would be stronger than the question requires. The relevant property is that independently changing speakers or microphones should not falsely activate pronunciation adaptation. Distances need not be identical in every circumstance for the gate to make the intended decision; conversely, small distance changes alone would not establish that false activations are absent.
Does “without false activations” specify an acceptable error rate?

No numerical false-activation tolerance is given in this question. It asks whether the distance-based trigger can avoid false activations under the stated independent changes. We should not turn that into a claimed measured rate, a chosen threshold, or a guarantee that the gate is perfect.
Could I answer yes just because distances provide a way to choose whether to activate?

No. A distance can supply a decision signal, but the existence of a signal does not establish that it identifies pronunciation shifts rather than speaker or microphone changes. A defensible answer would distinguish the proposed triggering mechanism from the still-unresolved question of false activations.
What is the most precise way to leave the question open?

You could ask: “Can distances to accent prototypes reliably select when to activate the pronunciation LoRA, without activating it merely because the speaker or microphone changes independently?” That retains both parts of the question—the intended pronunciation-related trigger and the concern about false activation—without presuming an answer.
My hypothesis is that speaker/channel-invariant accent prototypes will gate the pronunciation LoRA for at least 80% of unseen-accent utterances, but for no more than 5% of existing-accent utterances.

That states a predicted distinction in the gate’s behavior, not an observed result. The prototypes are intended to be insensitive to speaker and channel variation. Under the hypothesis, the gate would select the pronunciation LoRA for ≥80% of unseen-accent utterances and ≤5% of existing-accent utterances.
How does that relate to my question about false activations when speakers and microphones change independently?

It proposes an answer in terms of which utterances activate the LoRA: activation should be common for the unseen accent and uncommon for existing accents, despite the intended speaker/channel invariance of the prototypes. It does not yet establish that independent changes in speaker or microphone leave the gate unaffected. That remains part of what the hypothesis would need to bear out.
What exactly is being counted in those percentages?

The percentages refer to utterances for which the gate selects the pronunciation LoRA. The ≥80% figure uses unseen-accent utterances as its denominator; the ≤5% figure uses existing-accent utterances as its denominator. They are not percentages of words recognized correctly or amounts of WER improvement.
So the 5% is not five percentage points of WER?

Correct. It is an upper bound on the share of existing-accent utterances that activate the LoRA. A five-percent activation rate and a five-percentage-point WER increase describe different things; this hypothesis states only the activation-rate bound.
And does 80% mean the unseen-accent WER improves by 80%?

No. It predicts that the LoRA is selected for at least 80% of unseen-accent utterances. Whether recognition improves on those utterances, and by how much, is a separate question. The activation prediction does not imply the goal’s ≥15% relative unseen-accent WER reduction against the frozen recognizer.
Could both activation percentages hold while the adaptation still performs poorly?

Yes. The gate could select the LoRA at the predicted frequencies without the LoRA producing better recognition when selected. Likewise, a low existing-accent activation rate alone does not establish that existing-accent WER increases stay within one percentage point. The hypothesis concerns selection behavior, not the resulting recognition accuracy.
What does speaker/channel-invariant mean in this hypothesis?

It expresses the intended property of the accent prototypes: their relevance to the gate should not be driven by who is speaking or by the channel, including microphone changes. It is part of the hypothesis, not a demonstrated property or a specification of how invariance is obtained.
Does the hypothesis require every prototype distance to remain exactly the same across speakers and channels?

It does not specify exact equality of distances. The substantive prediction is about the gate: it should select the LoRA frequently for unseen-accent utterances and rarely for existing-accent utterances, with prototypes intended to resist speaker and channel variation. Exact numerical behavior of the distances is not given.
If an existing-accent utterance activates the LoRA, can I automatically call that a false activation?

The hypothesis treats existing-accent activation as something to keep uncommon, with a bound of ≤5%. But it does not define the correctness of every individual activation. It is more precise to say that the bound limits activation on existing-accent utterances, rather than asserting that each such activation has been shown to be false or harmful.
Does the hypothesis say what happens on utterances that do not activate it?

In the proposed gating arrangement, frozen decoding is retained otherwise. Thus the hypothesis predicts how often each accent category would take the LoRA path, while utterances for which the gate does not select it would remain on the frozen-decoding path. It does not predict the WER of either path.
At the 80% boundary, does that leave 20% of unseen-accent utterances without the LoRA?

If activation were exactly 80%, yes: the other 20% would not activate it. Because the prediction is at least 80%, the non-activating share could be 20% or less. This is simply the complement of the stated utterance-level activation rate, not a prediction about errors in that share.
And the existing-accent bound implies at least 95% retain frozen decoding?

Under the proposed choice between LoRA activation and frozen decoding otherwise, yes. If at most 5% of existing-accent utterances activate the LoRA, at least 95% do not. That still does not, by itself, determine the overall existing-accent WER.
Have we specified how to calculate prototype distances or where to place the gating cutoff?

No. The hypothesis specifies the intended speaker/channel-invariant prototypes and the predicted activation frequencies. It does not specify a distance formula, a cutoff, how prototypes are formed, or how the gate is calibrated. Those details should not be presented as already decided.
Should I describe the two numbers as measured performance?

No. They are hypothesized thresholds: ≥80% activation for unseen-accent utterances and ≤5% activation for existing-accent utterances. Saying they were measured or achieved would turn the hypothesis into an unsupported result.
Can you state the hypothesis in one sentence without making it sound proven?

We hypothesize that speaker/channel-invariant accent prototypes will cause the gate to select the pronunciation LoRA for at least 80% of unseen-accent utterances while selecting it for no more than 5% of existing-accent utterances.

To examine whether accent-prototype distances can trigger the pronunciation LoRA without false activations, I plan to train adversarial accent prototypes on unlabeled speech, calibrate the gate on existing accents, and measure activation and WER across crossed speakers and channels.

That is a plan for examining the gate, not a result. Training the prototypes on unlabeled speech addresses how the gate’s accent representation is developed. Calibrating on existing accents concerns when the gate selects adaptation rather than retaining frozen decoding. Measuring both activation and word error rate across crossed speakers and channels would show the gate’s choices alongside recognition performance when those two sources of variation are not tied together.
What does “adversarial accent prototypes” mean in this plan?

It describes prototypes trained with the aim of representing accent-related information while resisting speaker and channel variation. The plan specifies that they are trained adversarially on unlabeled speech, but it does not specify the adversarial objective, the training procedure, or how the prototypes are represented. Their intended invariance remains something to examine, not something the term alone establishes.
Does unlabeled speech apply to the prototype training specifically?

Yes. The plan explicitly says to train the adversarial accent prototypes on unlabeled speech. It does not say that transcripts are supplied for that training, nor does it lay out the complete data requirements for every other part of the plan.
Why calibrate the gate on existing accents?

Existing accents are where an inappropriate decision to activate the pronunciation LoRA could matter for preserving recognition performance. Calibrating the gate on them is intended to inform its decision boundary before examining how it behaves more broadly. The plan does not specify a calibration rule or claim that calibration will eliminate false activations.
Is gate calibration the same thing as retraining the pronunciation LoRA?

No. In this plan, calibration concerns the gate’s decision about whether to use the adaptation. Retraining the pronunciation LoRA would concern the adaptation component itself. The plan names prototype training and gate calibration, but does not say that calibrating the gate retrains the LoRA.
Are you assuming a particular numerical cutoff for prototype distance?

No. Calibrating a gate implies determining how its decision is made, but this plan gives no distance cutoff, calibration criterion, or decision formula. A specific value would be an added implementation detail, not part of the stated plan.
What does it mean to measure activation?

It means recording when the gate selects the pronunciation LoRA and when it leaves decoding on the frozen path. That measures the gate’s behavior directly. It is distinct from WER, which measures recognition errors rather than how often a particular decoding path was chosen.
Why measure WER as well as activation?

Activation alone cannot tell us whether the selected path helps recognition or harms it. WER supplies the corresponding recognition outcome. Considering both makes it possible to distinguish a gate that selects adaptation frequently from one whose selections are useful, without presuming that either pattern will occur.
Does measuring WER conflict with using unlabeled speech for training?

Not inherently. Training on unlabeled speech and evaluating WER are different activities: calculating WER requires a reference for assessment, whereas the plan says the accent prototypes are trained on unlabeled speech. The plan does not specify how evaluation references are obtained, and a reference used for evaluation should not be silently treated as training supervision.
What are crossed speakers and channels?

The phrase means examining speaker and channel variation in combination rather than treating each speaker as inseparable from one channel. It lets the measurements address what happens when the speaker changes, the channel changes, or both change. The plan does not specify the number of speakers, channels, or combinations to be measured.
Is a microphone change included in what you mean by a channel change?

A microphone change is a relevant example of channel variation for the gate question. The plan uses the broader term “channels,” so it should not be narrowed to microphones alone. The important condition is that channel and speaker differences can be examined separately.
Why isn't measuring only one speaker on each channel enough?

If each speaker appears only with one channel, a gate’s response to that pairing would not clearly distinguish the two sources of variation. Crossed speaker/channel measurements address the concern more directly by allowing their effects on activation and WER to be considered separately. That is the purpose of the crossing, not a claim about what the measurements will show.
Could the prototypes still appear accent-sensitive while reacting to the channel?

That is precisely a possibility the crossed measurements are meant to make visible. An apparent relationship between prototype-based activation and accent would not, by itself, show that channel variation has been separated out. Measuring activation while speakers and channels are crossed helps examine whether channel changes coincide with unwanted gate decisions.
Would WER alone reveal a false activation?

Not necessarily. WER describes recognition accuracy but does not directly report whether the gate activated the LoRA. Activation measurements identify which path was selected; WER measurements show how recognition performed. The plan calls for both rather than using one as a substitute for the other.
And would activation alone reveal damage to existing accents?

No. An activation count does not tell us the size or direction of a WER change. Measuring WER on existing accents is needed to assess recognition performance there; measuring activation helps interpret whether the gate selected the adaptation path. The plan does not assert that any measured change will occur.
Does calibrating on existing accents guarantee the gate will not activate for them?

No. Calibration is a planned step, not a guarantee of any particular activation behavior. The subsequent activation measurements are part of finding out how the calibrated gate behaves, including on existing accents under crossed speaker and channel variation.
Are the prototypes trained on existing accents only?

The plan says they are trained on unlabeled speech; it does not specify the accent composition of that speech. “On existing accents” describes the gate calibration step, not an explicit restriction on what speech is used to train the prototypes.
Does the plan prescribe an exact way of reporting activation and WER?

No. It specifies the quantities to measure and the crossed speaker/channel condition, but not an aggregation rule, reporting format, or numerical acceptance criterion for this measurement step. Those details should not be represented as already chosen.
Could I describe the plan as testing whether the prototypes are fully invariant?

It is more precise to say the plan examines whether prototype-based gating remains appropriately selective as speakers and channels vary independently. Training the prototypes adversarially aims at invariance, while measuring activation and WER across crossed speakers and channels examines behavior. The plan does not define or promise complete invariance.
What if the gate activates after a speaker change but WER stays the same?

Conceptually, the activation measurement would still flag that the gate’s decision changed, while the WER measurement would indicate no change in that recognition outcome. The two observations answer different questions. This is a hypothetical interpretation, not a reported outcome or a rule for classifying every activation.
What if WER changes even though the gate keeps frozen decoding?

That would illustrate why the crossed measurements matter: speaker and channel changes can affect recognition performance separately from a gate decision. Activation would show that the LoRA was not selected, while WER would show the recognition outcome. Again, that is a possible pattern to interpret, not an assertion that it occurs.
Does this plan by itself answer whether accent-prototype distances avoid false activations?

No. It lays out how to investigate that question: train adversarial accent prototypes on unlabeled speech, calibrate the gate on existing accents, then measure activation and WER with speakers and channels crossed. Whether distance-based gating avoids false activations is left to what those measurements show.
For this activity, train adversarial accent prototypes on unlabeled speech, then test gate activation for unseen and existing accents across 12 speakers crossed with four microphones.

That specifies prototype training and an activation test. The prototypes are to be trained adversarially on unlabeled speech. The test then examines whether the gate selects the pronunciation LoRA for unseen-accent and existing-accent utterances when speaker and microphone vary in crossed combinations. No activation results are stated yet.
What does “crossed” mean with 12 speakers and four microphones?

It means the speaker and microphone factors are combined rather than assigning each speaker a single, inseparable microphone. Twelve speakers crossed with four microphones gives 48 possible speaker–microphone combinations. The description does not say how many utterances are tested in each combination.
Why is that different from simply testing 12 speakers recorded on four microphones?

That wording could mean the speakers and microphones appear in the test without being systematically combined. “Crossed” makes the independent variation important: a speaker can be considered across microphones, and a microphone across speakers. That is relevant when asking whether a change in either factor affects the gate’s decision.
Are the 12 speakers all supposed to have the unseen accent?

The activity does not assign the 12 speakers to accent categories. It specifies testing activation for both unseen and existing accents across 12 speakers crossed with four microphones, but it does not give the number of speakers or utterances in either accent category.
Can I say there are 48 unseen-accent test utterances and 48 existing-accent test utterances?

No. Forty-eight is the number of possible speaker–microphone combinations from the stated crossing, not an utterance count for either accent category. The activity gives no number of utterances per combination or per accent.
What exactly is tested after the prototypes are trained?

The stated test is gate activation: whether the gate selects the pronunciation LoRA for unseen-accent utterances and for existing-accent utterances under the crossed speaker–microphone conditions. Training the prototypes and testing the gate’s selections are distinct parts of the activity.
Does testing activation also tell us how many words the recognizer gets wrong?

No. Activation records the gate’s choice; word error rate measures recognition errors. This activity specifically says to test gate activation. It does not state that WER is measured in this step, so an activation finding should not be described as a WER finding.
What is the point of including both unseen and existing accents in the activation test?

It lets the test examine both sides of the proposed gate behavior: whether the LoRA is selected for unseen-accent speech and whether it is selected for existing-accent speech. Looking at only one category would not describe how selectively the gate treats the two. The activity does not state what either activation rate turns out to be.
Is this the test of the hypothesis about activating for at least 80% of unseen-accent utterances and at most 5% of existing-accent utterances?

The activation test is relevant to that hypothesis. The ≥80% and ≤5% figures concern the proportions of utterances for which the gate selects the LoRA in the two accent categories. This activity describes where those selections are to be tested—across 12 speakers crossed with four microphones—but supplies no measured proportions or conclusion about the hypothesis.
Could I calculate the activation percentage from the 12 and four alone?

No. Those numbers describe speaker and microphone variation, not how often the gate activates. An activation percentage would require the gate’s decisions and the number of tested utterances in the relevant accent category. Neither is provided as a result here.
What does “adversarial” establish about the trained prototypes?

It describes the training approach and its intended resistance to speaker or channel variation; it does not establish that the resulting prototypes are invariant. The crossed-microphone activation test is useful precisely because the gate’s behavior under those changes remains to be examined.
Is a microphone the same thing as a channel in this activity?

The four microphones provide the specified form of channel variation in this activity. Speaker variation comes from the 12 speakers. That does not mean microphones exhaust every possible kind of channel variation; the activity names four microphones, not a broader inventory of channels.
If the same speaker appears on different microphones, what can the activation test tell us?

It can show whether the gate’s selection changes across those microphone conditions for that speaker’s tested utterances. Likewise, looking across speakers on a microphone can make speaker-related differences in selection visible. The activity does not prescribe a particular analysis or state what those comparisons will show.
Would any activation on an existing accent automatically prove that the adversarial training failed?

No. The activity tests how often the gate activates for existing accents, not whether a single activation proves a cause or settles the quality of the prototypes. Even the stated hypothesis allows activation for up to 5% of existing-accent utterances. The test would need actual observations before any conclusion could be drawn.
And if activation varies across microphones, can we immediately attribute it to the microphone?

The crossing helps distinguish microphone variation from speaker variation, but a difference in observed activation alone should not be overinterpreted as a complete causal explanation. This activity specifies the factors and the gate outcome to test; it does not supply results or a causal analysis.
Does this activity say how the gate is calibrated?

No. It specifies training adversarial prototypes on unlabeled speech and testing unseen- and existing-accent gate activation across the crossed speakers and microphones. It does not give a calibration procedure, prototype-distance formula, or activation threshold.
Can I report that the gate is robust to independently changing speakers and microphones once this test is set up?

Speaker/channel augmentation consistency is intended to keep the adapted phoneme-posterior behavior from following those sources of variation. They could place different pressures on an adaptation: one encourages a useful response to pronunciation differences, while the consistency and anchor terms discourage certain changes. The proposal does not specify how those pressures are balanced or report whether a conflict occurs in practice.
Are we committed to a particular loss function or weight for either constraint?

No. Preserving existing-accent WER does not determine whether unseen-accent WER decreases. Both predicted outcomes require their own frozen-versus-adapted comparison.

I propose building a speaker/channel-invariant, pseudo-labeled phonetic exemplar memory from unlabeled augmentations, then using it to acoustically rescore frozen hypotheses with conservative fallback.

That proposes an exemplar-based adaptation path. The memory would hold phonetic examples associated with pseudo-labels derived from unlabeled, augmented speech, with the intended property that speaker and channel differences do not dominate the representation. It would inform acoustic rescoring among hypotheses from the frozen recognizer, while conservative fallback would limit when a changed selection is accepted. What is a phonetic exemplar memory supposed to store?

At the conceptual level, it stores examples of phonetic patterns that the rescoring step can consult when judging frozen-recognizer hypotheses. The proposal does not specify the form of an exemplar, the size of the memory, the phonetic units used, or a retrieval method. Calling it phonetic states the intended focus rather than verifying the correctness of every stored example.
Does pseudo-labeled mean the adaptation speech has reference phoneme transcripts?

No. Pseudo-labels are inferred labels rather than supplied ground-truth phoneme annotations. The speech used for this proposed adaptation remains unlabeled; generating a hypothesis for an exemplar does not make that hypothesis verified.
Could the pseudo-labels be wrong?

Yes. Their correctness is not guaranteed by the proposal. An erroneous pseudo-label could affect what the memory appears to represent, which is one reason not to treat the memory as a collection of known, correctly labeled pronunciations.
What do ‘unlabeled augmentations’ contribute?

They supply augmented versions of unlabeled speech from which the pseudo-labeled exemplars would be built. The intended benefit is to keep the memory focused on phonetic information that is useful despite speaker or channel changes. The proposal does not identify the augmentations, how many are made, or how pseudo-labels are assigned across them.
Are the augmentations definitely microphone simulations and new-speaker synthesis?

No. Those would be specific implementation choices. The proposal says only ‘unlabeled augmentations’ and calls for speaker/channel invariance; it does not prescribe the transformations used to represent either kind of variation.
Does speaker/channel-invariant mean the same acoustic recording is stored for everyone?

No. It is an intended property of what the memory captures or how it is used: accent-related phonetic information should remain relevant when speaker or channel differs. It does not mean recordings become identical, and the proposal does not specify a numerical invariance criterion.
Could a memory built from augmentations still track the microphone?

Potentially. Augmentation is intended to discourage that dependence, but its inclusion does not prove channel invariance. Whether an exemplar or a rescoring decision follows a microphone effect rather than a phonetic pattern would need to be assessed rather than assumed.
What does acoustically rescoring frozen hypotheses mean?

The frozen recognizer supplies candidate hypotheses, and the proposed memory would provide acoustic information used to reconsider their relative preference. Rescoring can change which available hypothesis is preferred; as stated, it does not create a candidate that the frozen recognizer never supplied. The proposal does not specify a score or how it is combined with the frozen recognizer’s own ranking.
So is the memory changing the recognizer’s acoustic model weights?

That is not stated. The proposal describes a phonetic exemplar memory used for acoustic rescoring of frozen hypotheses. It does not call for changing the frozen recognizer’s weights or identify any trainable recognizer component.
Is rescoring the same as correcting the text after the recognizer finishes?

Not as described here. Rescoring selects among frozen-recognizer hypotheses using additional acoustic information. A separate text-rewriting step that can introduce new words is not part of the stated proposal.
What if the correct word is absent from every frozen hypothesis?

A rescoring-only mechanism cannot select a hypothesis that is not available among the frozen candidates. That is a general limitation of the proposed scope. The proposal does not add candidate generation, so any recognition gain would have to come from choosing better among the available hypotheses.
What does conservative fallback mean in this proposal?

It expresses an intent to retain the frozen recognizer’s selection when the exemplar-based acoustic evidence is not sufficient to justify changing it. The proposal does not define the sufficiency criterion, a numerical threshold, or the exact fallback procedure. It should not be treated as a guarantee of no errors or no existing-accent WER increase.
Does fallback mean the memory is never used on existing accents?

No such accent-specific rule is stated. Conservative fallback limits changes when its unspecified condition calls for retaining the frozen selection, but the proposal does not say that the memory is categorically disabled for existing-accent utterances.
If fallback occurs, does that prove the frozen hypothesis is correct?

No. It means the proposed adaptation does not override that frozen choice in that case. The frozen recognizer can still make mistakes; fallback is a decision to avoid an insufficiently supported change, not a verification of the original hypothesis.
How is the memory meant to relate to pronunciation shifts?

The intended use is to capture phonetic evidence relevant to accent-related pronunciation differences and use it when comparing frozen hypotheses. Speaker/channel invariance is proposed so those phonetic examples remain useful across people and recording conditions rather than reflecting those differences. The proposal does not establish that the memory actually isolates accent-related shifts.
Would acoustically rescoring hypotheses by itself establish the adaptation is unsupervised?

The unlabeled condition comes from how the memory is built: pseudo-labeled exemplars from unlabeled augmentations rather than supplied adaptation transcripts. Rescoring is the proposed way to use that memory. The proposal does not say that the frozen recognizer was originally trained without supervision.
Can we say this approach has already reduced unseen-accent WER?
No. This is a proposal and gives no WER measurement. The relevant goal is at least a 15% relative reduction in unseen-accent WER against the frozen recognizer using only unlabeled adaptation speech.
And does conservative fallback already ensure the existing-accent limit?

No. Rescoring can still change recognition on some existing-accent speech, and a conservative intent is not a measured WER bound. The existing-accent requirement remains an increase of no more than one percentage point when speakers and channels vary independently.
Does this proposal require an accent-prototype gate, a pronunciation LoRA, or a lattice transducer?

None of those is specified as a required component. The named mechanism is a pseudo-labeled phonetic exemplar memory built from unlabeled augmentations, used to acoustically rescore frozen hypotheses with conservative fallback. Adding another adaptation component would be a separate design choice.
Can I say the memory contains verified accent-specific pronunciations?

No. Its labels are pseudo-labels, and the proposal gives no verification result. It is intended to represent phonetic patterns relevant to adaptation, not described as a ground-truth pronunciation inventory.
What is the careful one-sentence version of the proposal?

Build a speaker/channel-invariant phonetic exemplar memory using pseudo-labels from unlabeled augmented speech, and use its acoustic evidence to rescore the frozen recognizer’s available hypotheses while falling back conservatively when that evidence does not justify a change.

For the exemplar-memory approach, I plan to build augmentation-invariant phonetic exemplars, rescore frozen beams with confidence-gated retrieval, and then test WER across held-out speaker–microphone crosses.

That is a proposed sequence, not an outcome: construct phonetic exemplars intended to remain useful under augmentation, retrieve them conditionally to inform acoustic rescoring of the frozen recognizer’s beams, and evaluate the resulting word error rate across held-out speaker–microphone combinations. The plan gives neither a retrieval confidence rule nor any WER values.
What does augmentation-invariant mean for an exemplar?

It names an intended property: the exemplar’s phonetic relevance should persist under the variations represented by augmentation, rather than being tied to incidental differences in a recording. The plan does not specify the augmentations, an invariance measure, or evidence that the constructed exemplars achieve that property.
Is the plan claiming all exemplars will be identical under augmentation?

No. Invariance in the intended sense does not require the stored acoustic examples or their representations to be numerically identical. The plan does not prescribe exact equality or any tolerance for differences across augmented versions.
Are speaker and microphone changes the variations we care about?

They are the named factors in the held-out evaluation crosses, and the exemplar approach is intended to separate phonetic pronunciation information from speaker and channel variation. The plan itself does not specify a list of augmentations or state that microphone changes exhaust all possible channel differences.
Does building exemplars mean they are already correctly labeled phonemes?

No. The exemplar-memory proposal uses pseudo-labeled material from unlabeled augmentations. An exemplar’s phonetic label is an inferred hypothesis, not a verified phoneme annotation. Constructing the exemplars does not by itself establish that each label is correct.
Is the plan asking us to train the frozen recognizer again?
No. Its beams are the candidate hypotheses to be rescored. The plan does not call for retraining the frozen recognizer or changing how it generates those candidates.
What happens during confidence-gated retrieval?

The gate determines whether retrieved phonetic exemplars are used to inform rescoring of the frozen beam candidates. The plan does not state where a confidence score comes from, what cutoff is applied, or how retrieval and rescoring are calculated. It identifies a conditional use of the memory rather than unconditional reliance on every retrieved example.
Does the confidence gate test whether a pseudo-label is correct?

That is not specified. Confidence-gated retrieval controls when exemplar information is used, but no confidence target or verification mechanism is given. It should not be described as certifying the pseudo-labels.
When the gate declines retrieval, do we still rescore the frozen beams?

The intended role of the gate is to permit or withhold exemplar-based rescoring. If retrieval is withheld, those exemplars do not alter the frozen beam ranking through this proposed mechanism. The plan does not specify any other rescoring component or an additional decoding change.
Does rescoring permit us to add a word that never appeared in the frozen beam?
Not as stated. Rescoring changes the relative preference among existing frozen-beam hypotheses. It does not describe a mechanism for generating new hypotheses or inserting a missing candidate.
Why make retrieval conditional instead of using the closest exemplar every time?

The confidence gate is intended to limit changes based on potentially uncertain pseudo-labeled exemplars. Using an exemplar whenever one is retrievable could allow weak or mismatched evidence to affect a frozen decision. That is the design rationale, not a finding that the gate correctly accepts or rejects any particular retrieval.
Is there a specified fallback threshold or required margin over frozen decoding?
No numerical confidence cutoff, margin, or fallback criterion is stated. The plan calls for confidence-gated retrieval when rescoring frozen beams, but its exact decision rule remains unspecified.
Does conservative fallback mean existing-accent beams can never be reordered?

No. The proposal’s conservative fallback describes an intent to avoid insufficiently supported changes, not a categorical ban on reranking existing-accent utterances. The plan does not give a separate gate rule by accent category or guarantee zero existing-accent WER drift.
What will the WER test tell us?

It will measure recognition errors for the resulting exemplar-based rescoring approach on held-out speaker–microphone crosses. The broader goal calls for improving unseen-accent WER while limiting any increase on existing accents, but the plan does not supply those measurements or specify a per-cross reporting format.
Why test across crossed speakers and microphones instead of treating each recorded voice as one condition?

Crossing the two factors keeps speaker changes distinguishable from microphone changes. That is relevant to an exemplar memory intended to reflect phonetic pronunciation rather than characteristics of a particular speaker or recording channel. The plan does not say how many speakers or microphones appear or that every possible pair must be present.
Does ‘held-out crosses’ mean the same speakers and microphones were never seen while building the memory?

Not necessarily. It identifies speaker–microphone combinations reserved for evaluation, but does not say whether their individual speakers, individual microphones, or only particular pairings were absent during memory construction. The exact holdout scheme is not provided.
Should I state that the test is on unseen and existing accents separately?

The broader goal requires both: an unseen-accent WER reduction relative to frozen recognition and protection of existing-accent WER. This plan says to test WER across held-out speaker–microphone crosses, without explicitly prescribing a particular table layout or accent-specific aggregation. It is important not to claim either accent outcome before measurement.
Can we compute WER on the same unlabeled material used to build exemplars?

WER requires reference words, while the memory-building material is described as unlabeled. The plan’s WER test is on held-out crosses, so it should be distinguished from building the exemplar memory. It does not explain how evaluation references are obtained or authorize using them as labels for memory construction.
Would a good WER result prove the memory is speaker/channel-invariant?

It would show a recognition outcome under the evaluated speaker–microphone conditions. It would not, by itself, prove that every exemplar representation excludes speaker and channel information or that each retrieval is based only on phonetic similarity.
What would count as meeting the unseen-accent part of the goal?

The goal requires at least a 15% relative reduction in unseen-accent WER against the frozen recognizer using only unlabeled adaptation speech. The plan proposes exemplar-based rescoring and a WER test, but does not report whether that numerical comparison is met.
And the existing-accent part?

Existing-accent WER increases must be limited to one percentage point under independently varying speakers and channels. Confidence-gated retrieval may be intended to protect the frozen recognizer’s behavior, but only the measured WER change can establish its size. The plan provides no such change.
What is a concise, faithful description of the plan?

Build phonetic exemplars intended to be augmentation-invariant, use confidence-gated retrieval of those exemplars to acoustically rescore frozen beams, and test the resulting WER across held-out speaker–microphone crosses, without presuming a benefit or a preservation result.
